446: Customs' treatment of NAFTA §1520(d) refund claims: whether Customs gave a reasonable explanation for waiving the certificate-of-origin filing requirement for reconciliation claims but not traditional claims; Trade Court upheld Customs' remand explanation under Chevron.
That alone is a reasonable explanation for the difference in treatment between traditional claims and reconciliation-based claims.
536: Country-of-origin marking under 19 C.F.R. § 134.47: whether 'trademark' in § 134.47 unambiguously includes unregistered marks without a pending application, so that the more lenient marking rule applies to the pre-application and no-application jeans.
We hold that the term “trademark” in § 134.47 is clear on its face.
705: Denial of non-statutory equitable prejudgment interest on unpaid antidumping duties; Trade Court's discretionary weighing affirmed, so no equitable interest awarded on top of 6% §580 interest.
We see no abuse of discretion in its weighing of relevant factors and thus affirm the Trade Court's decision not to award equitable prejudgment interest.
706: Whether §580 statutory interest may be assessed on the bond amount including §1505(d) interest; held yes.
We hold that § 580 interest may be assessed on the bond up to its face value, including applicable § 1505(d) interest.
707: Start date for §580 interest: held to run from the government's first formal demand for payment, not from the post-protest demand.
The Trade Court did not err in holding that § 580 interest runs from the date of the government's first formal demand for payment.
709: Surety waived right to contest §1505(d) interest by failing to protest Customs' denial and challenge liability under §1514 finality of liquidation.
We hold that pursuant to § 1514(a), AHAC waived the right to appeal the application of § 1505(d) interest by failing to challenge its liability below.
3227: Section 1592 customs penalty: the Government may not independently bring a negligence penalty claim in the CIT where Customs asserted only gross negligence, because each culpability level is a separate claim that must be pursued administratively.
The Government cannot bring a penalty claim based on negligence in court because such a claim did not exist at the administrative level.
3359: Customs liability under continuous bond: 2005 reliquidations became final and conclusive because the surety did not timely protest or challenge them, so the surety is liable on the bond for antidumping duties.
We agree with the Court of International Trade that AHAC is liable to the government under the continuous bond.
3360: Whether 19 U.S.C. § 580 statutory prejudgment interest applies to bonds securing antidumping duties.
We hold, as a matter of law, that 19 U.S.C. § 580 provides for interest on bonds securing both traditional customs duties and antidumping duties.
3361: Entitlement to equitable prejudgment interest in addition to statutory interest; the Court of International Trade's award was vacated and remanded for the court to decide the issue in the first instance.

we think that the best approach is to vacate the Court of International Trade's award of equitable prejudgment interest and remand the case to the court so that it, in the first instance, may determine the issue of the government's entitlement to equitable prejudgment interest.
3636: Whether 'articles' in 19 U.S.C. § 1337 covers electronically transmitted digital data (scope of importable articles under Section 337 and customs-related import coverage).
we conclude that 'articles' does not cover electronically transmitted digital data.
3829: Whether the April 4, 2013 revocation instructions' phrase 'unliquidated entries' covered ThyssenKrupp's November/December 2012 liquidated entries so that antidumping duties were not owed on them (customs liquidation and protest issue).

the better reading of the statute is that entries covered by liquidation determinations that are still subject to alteration through ordinary direct review mechanisms are 'unliquidated entries' entitled to the benefit of the revocation order.
5257: Whether Commerce properly instructed CBP to continue suspending liquidation of Quiedan's entries, including entries made before the scope ruling, under 19 C.F.R. § 351.225(l).
It is similarly clear that continued suspension of liquidation is proper, at least where the scope ruling confirms a clear meaning.
5272: Customs protest issue: whether Customs' denial of retroactive GSP duty-free treatment on untimely entries was a protestable decision under 19 U.S.C. § 1514 or a nondiscretionary ministerial act.
Therefore, Customs' application of the deadline to Industrial Chemicals' untimely request was ministerial.
5850: Customs authority to suspend liquidation of entries based on an ambiguous antidumping/countervailing duty order, and whether Commerce could instruct continued suspension of liquidation for pre-scope-inquiry entries (en banc issue).

we break from the CIT and the prior panel opinion in this case, and now hold that Customs did not exceed its authority by ordering the suspension of liquidation based on its interpretation of the Orders.
6391: Counterfeit certification mark: Customs properly determined that PREMIUM model butane canisters bearing UL's certification mark were counterfeit under 19 U.S.C. 1526(e) and 15 U.S.C. 1127 at the time of importation, so the redelivery demand was lawful.

The record shows that ICCS's use of UL's certification mark on the date of entry falsely communicated to consumers that the imported PREMIUM model merchandise had already passed UL's safety standards and requirements.
6392: Customs' reliance on the trademark owner's consent: Customs did not improperly delegate its enforcement duty to UL or become an enforcement arm of private interests, because 1526(e) requires contacting the owner upon seizure and forfeiture is conditioned on the owner's absence of written consent; ICCS's remedy arguments were also rejected.
Thus, Customs was required by statute to contact UL upon seizure of ICCS's merchandise to ascertain whether or not UL consented to the use of its mark under the circumstances.
6754: Customs and Commerce authority to suspend liquidation and collect cash deposits on Sunpreme's entries made before the scope inquiry was initiated; court held Customs acted ultra vires and Commerce could not continue that suspension, so the pre-inquiry deposits for those entries are refundable to the importer.

We also affirm the CIT's determination that Commerce's instructions to Customs are invalid to the extent that they command continuation of suspension of liquidation and collection of cash deposits on Sunpreme's solar modules entered or withdrawn from warehouse for consumption before Commerce initiated its scope inquiry on December 30, 2015.
7313: Other customs issue: whether the tenth-digit statistical suffix (2924.19.11.50 'Other: Amides') could apply to ATBS under Subheading Note 1; court held statistical suffixes are not statutory and a non-amide cannot fall within the Amides subheading.
The first problem with Chemtall's argument is that the tenth-digit statistical suffixes, including the suffixes for acrylamide and "other" amides, are not statutory.
7823: Timeliness of Customs liquidation and reliquidation under 19 U.S.C. 1504(d) and 1501; the court held the notice date was May 30, 2017, so the entries were liquidated or reliquidated within the statutory window.

We conclude that the Court of International Trade correctly determined that its decision in the AFMC litigation did not provide such unambiguous and public notice, and that there is no genuine dispute of fact as to the notice date.
7824: Customs mislabeling of the December 1, 2017 notice for AFI's Tenth Subject Entry as a liquidation rather than a reliquidation was held harmless because no cognizable harm was alleged.
Accordingly, we agree with the Court of International Trade's decision that the labeling error was harmless.
8024: Customs treatment previously accorded under 19 U.S.C. § 1625(c): the Trade Court erred in allowing bypass entries (liquidated without examination or Customs officer review) to be considered in determining whether a treatment previously accorded existed; vacated and remanded for a determination excluding those entries.
In conclusion, the Trade Court erred in its construction of § 177.12(c)(1)(ii) as allowing consideration of bypass entries in the determination of whether there was a treatment previously accorded.
8025: Customs de facto established and uniform practice (EUP) under 19 U.S.C. § 1315(d): no clear abuse of discretion in finding no de facto EUP; affirmed.
Kent has failed to show a clear abuse of discretion in denying its claim of a de facto EUP.
9171: Validity of a 2018 Treasury/CBP Rule defining drawback to include excise tax on exports never paid or determined, and limiting drawback to taxes paid; the court held the Rule contrary to the unambiguous text of 19 U.S.C. § 1313(v) at Chevron step one and affirmed its invalidation.

We conclude that the challenged provisions of the Rule contravene the unambiguous text of the statute and, therefore, the inquiry ends at Chevron step one. Accordingly, we affirm the judgment of the CIT that the Rule is unlawful as to the challenged provisions.
10643: Other customs valuation: whether first-sale (manufacturer) price is a viable transaction value under 19 U.S.C. §1401a and Nissho Iwai, given the nonmarket-influence requirement imposed by the trial court; court held the trial court misread Nissho Iwai and vacated and remanded.

The trial court misinterpreted Nissho Iwai to impose a requirement beyond what the statute and regulations demand, so we vacate and remand for the trial court to reconsider whether Meyer may rely on its first-sale prices.
11531: Drawback claim deemed-liquidation timing under 19 U.S.C. § 1504(a)(2)(A) and (B): Customs' April 30, 2021 liquidation at zero drawback was lawful because subparagraph (B) governed the claim whose import entries were liquidated but not final, so no automatic deemed liquidation occurred under (A).
We hold that under the plain text of the statute, subparagraph (A) does not apply when the conditions set forth in (B) are present.
12459: Customs liquidation instructions: whether Commerce was required to revoke its suspension-of-liquidation instructions to Customs after the remand and initiation of a subsection (e) scope inquiry.
we are thus unpersuaded Commerce erred in not revoking its liquidation instructions to Customs and affirm the Trade Court's decision holding the same.
13032: Customs liquidation finality under 19 U.S.C. 1514 and whether the CIT could order reliquidation of entries after the 90-day window in 1501, applying Cemex; the court held the CIT erred in ordering reliquidation, favoring the importer.
This case is governed by Cemex, and the CIT erred by concluding otherwise.
14419: Country of origin: whether the xanthan gum was Chinese-origin transshipped through India, and whether the evasion determination was supported by substantial evidence; held supported by substantial evidence.
Customs' determination of evasion is supported by substantial evidence.
14751: Customs liquidation: whether Customs properly extended the liquidation period under 19 U.S.C. 1504(b)(1) and the entries were not deemed liquidated by operation of law; extension held not an abuse of discretion.
We therefore affirm the CIT's ruling that Customs did not abuse its discretion in extending liquidation and that the entries in question were not liquidated by operation of law.
14752: Customs valuation: whether domestic sales can be sales for exportation to the United States under 19 U.S.C. 1401a(b)(1) so that transaction value applies; held that transaction value is the proper basis of appraisement.

The CIT correctly decided that 19 U.S.C. §1401a(b)(1) does not require an international sale or a sale abroad to have occurred for a sale of merchandise to be considered as a sale "for exportation to the United States."
14773: Customs transaction valuation for related-party sales: whether Meyer may rely on the first-sale price under 19 U.S.C. § 1401a(b)(2)(B) and 19 C.F.R. § 152.103(l)(1). The court held the trial court failed to reconsider the question on the record and vacated the denial of first-sale treatment for reconsideration.

Because the Court of International Trade failed to meaningfully evaluate whether Meyer was entitled to rely on first-sale price in accordance with our remand order, we again vacate and remand for the court to reconsider whether Meyer may rely on the first-sale price.
